headline: Hundreds feared trapped in Nepal flood tunnels

sources.title: Nepal tunnel traps hinder flood rescue: How many are dead or missing?
Search for hundreds in hydropower tunnels in Nepal
Hundreds trapped underground after Nepal flood disaster (DW News, video)

chunks.text: One week after Nepal's glacier flood, rescuers face a new [[emergency]]. Hundreds of workers are believed trapped inside tunnels at [[hydropower]] projects on the flooded rivers. When the [[flash flood]] hit on August 26, mud and debris {{piled up}} at the [[entrances]] and {{blocked them off}}, sealing the workers inside. About 900 workers were at sites in the [[flood zone]]. Those at about six tunnels are [[feared]] trapped, most at the Trishuli projects in Rasuwa district.

verbs.correct: To collect in a large heap
verbs.wrong: To wash slowly down a river
verbs.why: Dirty dishes pile up in the sink after a party, and unread emails pile up over a long weekend. Here mud and debris piled up at the tunnel entrances when the flood hit.

verbs.correct: To close a way so nothing can pass
verbs.wrong: To mark a route as safe to use
verbs.why: Police block off a street for a parade, and a fallen tree can block off a country road. The flood's mud blocked off the tunnel entrances and sealed the workers inside.

chunks.text: Rescue [[crews]] are working [[day and night]] to {{clear away}} the mud, by hand and with machines. A Nepal Army [[spokesperson]] said a large amount of debris had been [[deposited]] there, "posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels." Where crews have managed to {{break through}}, they have {{sent in}} oxygen through small openings. Nearly 300 workers have already been {{brought out}} alive, but a few bodies have also been [[recovered]] from the tunnels.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a place
verbs.wrong: To measure how deep the mud is
verbs.why: We clear away the plates after dinner, and crews clear away snow from a runway before a flight. Rescue crews are now clearing away the mud by hand and with heavy machines.

verbs.correct: To force a way past a barrier
verbs.wrong: To make a dark space brighter
verbs.why: A drill can break through a concrete wall, and the sun breaks through the clouds after a storm. Where crews have managed to break through, they have reached the workers inside.

verbs.correct: To pass something into a closed space
verbs.wrong: To count the people in a group
verbs.why: A coach sends in a fresh player late in the game, and a company sends in engineers to fix a broken machine. Rescuers sent in oxygen through small openings to the trapped workers.

verbs.correct: To carry someone from inside a place
verbs.wrong: To treat an injury on the spot
verbs.why: Firefighters bring out people from a smoky building, and divers bring out sailors from a sunken boat. Nearly 300 workers have already been brought out of the tunnels alive.

chunks.text: Six days after the disaster, officials say they are in a [[race against time]]. The biggest fear is [[suffocation]]: the workers still trapped could {{run out of}} air, and they have little or no food and water. Nobody knows how long they can {{hold out}}. Outside the tunnels, [[relatives]] of the missing workers are waiting for news. Rescue teams have not {{given up}}, and the digging continues.

verbs.correct: To have no more of something
verbs.why: A car runs out of gas on a long trip, and a store runs out of bread before a storm. Officials fear the trapped workers could run out of air, food, and water.

verbs.correct: To stay alive in a hard situation
verbs.wrong: To call for help with a radio
verbs.why: Lost hikers can hold out for days on very little food, and a small town held out through a long winter without power. Nobody knows how long the trapped workers can hold out underground.
A runner with a sore knee refuses to give up before the finish line, and a student keeps studying instead of giving up on a hard exam. Rescue teams have not given up, and the digging continues.

chunks.text: The tunnel rescue is part of a larger [[operation]]. The flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, and over a dozen in Tibet. Thousands are still missing, including hundreds of [[foreign nationals]]. Nearly 21,000 [[security personnel]] and [[volunteers]] have {{pitched in}}. China {{flew in}} more than 2,000 rescue workers and dropped [[equipment]] from the air, and India sent army officers trained in tunnel rescue. Crews now hope to {{step up}} the search. For the workers still [[underground]], every hour counts.

verbs.correct: To join others in doing the work
verbs.wrong: To build a camp for shelter
verbs.why: Neighbors pitch in to clean a park after a storm, and the whole family pitches in to cook a holiday dinner. Nearly 21,000 security personnel and volunteers have pitched in to help with the rescue.

verbs.wrong: To drop supplies from the sky
verbs.why: A hospital can fly in a rare medicine from another city, and a company flies in experts for a big repair job. China flew in more than 2,000 rescue workers to help Nepal.
A school steps up security after a theft, and a city steps up cleaning during flu season. With more help arriving, crews hope to step up the search for the missing workers.

mainIdea.s: A week after Nepal's glacier flood, rescuers are trying to reach hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in mud-blocked tunnels. Crews fear the workers could run out of air before help arrives.
mainIdea.why: Mud and debris blocked off the tunnel entrances, nearly 300 workers have been brought out, and suffocation is now the biggest fear for those still inside.

mainIdea.s: A new flood in Nepal's mountains has trapped hundreds of hydropower workers inside tunnels this week. Rescuers say the workers have enough air and food to wait safely for several more days.
mainIdea.why: Close, but there was no new flood. The workers were trapped by the August 26 flood, and officials fear they could run out of air, food, and water.

mainIdea.s: A tunnel collapsed during construction of a new hydropower dam in northern India, trapping about forty workers. Rescue teams drilled through solid rock for two weeks before reaching them.
mainIdea.why: This describes a different event. The workers here are in Nepal, trapped by flood mud, and India sent officers to help with the rescue.

tf.s: Mud and debris blocked off the tunnel entrances after the flood.
tf.why: The flash flood buried the entrances under thick mud and debris, sealing the workers inside.

tf.s: Nearly 300 workers have already been brought out alive.
tf.why: Rescuers have reached some of the tunnels, though a few bodies have also been recovered from inside.

tf.s: Rescue crews are clearing the mud only with heavy machines.
tf.why: Crews are clearing away the mud both by hand and with machines, and an army spokesperson called the debris a big challenge.

tf.s: Officials fear the trapped workers could run out of air.
tf.why: Suffocation is now the biggest fear, along with a lack of food and water for those still inside.

tf.s: China sent about 200 rescue workers to Nepal.
tf.why: China flew in more than 2,000 rescue workers and dropped equipment from the air.

tf.s: Fewer than 500 people have died in Nepal so far.
tf.why: The flood has now killed more than 900 people in Nepal, and thousands are still listed as missing.

lines.text: Have you been following the Nepal flood news? There's a new problem now. Hundreds of workers are trapped inside tunnels.
Tunnels? I thought the flood was in the river valleys.
It was. But there were hydropower projects along those rivers, and the workers were inside the tunnels when the flood hit. Mud and debris {{piled up}} at the entrances and {{blocked them off}}.
So they've been in there since last week? [[What a nightmare]].
Six days. Crews are trying to {{clear away}} the mud by hand and with machines, but an army spokesperson said the amount of debris is a huge challenge.
In some places, yes. Where crews managed to {{break through}}, they {{sent in}} oxygen through small openings. And nearly 300 workers have already been {{brought out}} alive.
That's something, at least. But the rest are [[not out of the woods yet]].
No. Officials fear they could {{run out of}} air before the tunnels are open. Food and water too.
How long can a person {{hold out}} like that?
Nobody really knows. [[The clock is ticking]], and that's why nobody wants to {{give up}}.
What about the families? Do they know anything?
Mostly they're just waiting outside the tunnels, [[completely in the dark]]. [[That's the part that gets me]].
Is anyone helping Nepal with this?
Nearly 21,000 soldiers, police, and volunteers have {{pitched in}}. China {{flew in}} more than 2,000 rescue workers, and India sent army officers trained in tunnel rescue.
I hope all of that helps them {{step up}} the search before it's too late.

expressions.def: Used to react to a situation that is terrible to think about

expressions.expr: not out of the woods yet

expressions.def: Used to say that very little time is left and pressure is growing

expressions.def: Knowing nothing about what is happening

expressions.expr: That's the part that gets me
expressions.def: Used to say that one detail affects you emotionally more than the rest
ex: He walked to work for a year to save money. That's the part that gets me.
The dog waited at the door every night. That's the part that gets me.
